q: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of weight loss, palpitations and heat intolerance. On examination she has a fine tremor, a diffuse smooth goitre with an audible bruit, and bilateral proptosis with lid lag. Her pulse is 112 bpm and regular. Investigations show: TSH <0.01 mU/L (0.3–4.2), free T4 38 pmol/L (9–25), free T3 12 pmol/L (3.5–6.5). TSH-receptor antibodies are strongly positive. Which single mechanism best explains this patient's ophthalmopathy?
options: Deposition of thyroxine within extraocular muscle fibres
TSH-receptor antibody stimulation of orbital fibroblasts causing glycosaminoglycan accumulation
Compressive optic neuropathy from an enlarged thyroid gland
Sympathetic overactivity causing levator palpebrae retraction alone
explain: This is Graves' disease with thyroid eye disease. 👁️ Orbital fibroblasts express the TSH receptor; stimulating TSH-receptor antibodies (and IGF-1 receptor cross-talk) activate these fibroblasts, driving glycosaminoglycan (GAG) accumulation, retro-orbital oedema, adipogenesis and lymphocytic infiltration of the extraocular muscles. The resulting increase in orbital contents within the bony orbit produces proptosis, periorbital swelling and, in severe cases, restrictive myopathy and compressive optic neuropathy. This is a genuinely infiltrative/autoimmune process — distinct from the sympathetically-mediated lid retraction and lid lag seen in any cause of thyrotoxicosis. Management follows NICE and EUGOGO principles: smoking cessation (smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor), selenium in mild disease, and IV glucocorticoids ± orbital radiotherapy or decompression for active moderate-to-severe or sight-threatening disease. Rendering the patient euthyroid is essential, and radioiodine can transiently worsen eye disease. Lid retraction alone (option E) reflects sympathetic tone but does not explain the proptosis.

The resulting increase in orbital contents within the bony orbit produces proptosis, periorbital swelling and, in severe cases, restrictive myopathy and compressive optic neuropathy. This is a genuinely infiltrative/autoimmune process — distinct from the sympathetically-mediated lid retraction and lid lag seen in any cause of thyrotoxicosis. Rendering the patient euthyroid is essential, and radioiodine can transiently worsen eye disease. Lid retraction alone (option E) reflects sympathetic tone but does not explain the proptosis.

A.text: Thyroxine is not deposited within muscle fibres. The extraocular muscle enlargement in Graves' orbitopathy is due to fibroblast activation, glycosaminoglycan deposition and lymphocytic infiltration, not accumulation of the hormone itself.

B.html: Correct. TSH-receptor antibodies stimulate orbital fibroblasts (which express the TSH receptor), causing GAG accumulation, oedema, adipogenesis and muscle infiltration. This expands orbital contents, producing proptosis and, when severe, compressive optic neuropathy.

C.html: The goitre is in the neck; it does not compress the orbit. Optic neuropathy in thyroid eye disease arises from crowding at the orbital apex by swollen extraocular muscles, not from the thyroid gland itself.

E.html: Sympathetic tone explains lid retraction and lid lag, which occur in any thyrotoxicosis, but cannot account for true proptosis, extraocular muscle enlargement or diplopia, which are specific to Graves' orbitopathy.

q: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 64 mmol/mol on metformin 1 g twice daily) attends for review. He has established heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (NYHA II) and stage 3a chronic kidney disease (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73m²). His BMI is 31 kg/m² and blood pressure 134/82 mmHg. He is keen to avoid hypoglycaemia and weight gain. According to current NICE type 2 diabetes guidance, which is the most appropriate additional agent?
explain: NICE (NG28, updated) recommends offering an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit to people with type 2 diabetes and established heart failure or chronic kidney disease, either at diagnosis or when intensifying therapy. 💙 This man has HFrEF and CKD — precisely the group in whom SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) reduce heart-failure hospitalisation, slow CKD progression and cut cardiovascular death, as shown in DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced and DAPA-CKD. These benefits are largely independent of glucose lowering. Dapagliflozin is licensed for HFrEF and CKD and is appropriate at this eGFR. It is weight-neutral to weight-losing and carries minimal hypoglycaemia risk, matching his preferences. Counsel on euglycaemic DKA (sick-day rules), genital mycotic infection and volume status. Gliclazide and insulin both cause weight gain and hypoglycaemia; pioglitazone is contraindicated in heart failure due to fluid retention; sitagliptin (a DPP-4 inhibitor) is weight-neutral but confers no cardiovascular or renal outcome benefit and saxagliptin specifically increased HF hospitalisation.

A.html: Gliclazide is effective and cheap but causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia, both of which he wishes to avoid, and provides no cardiovascular or renal outcome benefit in this high-risk patient.
A.text: Gliclazide is effective and cheap but causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia, both of which he wishes to avoid, and provides no cardiovascular or renal outcome benefit in this high-risk patient.

B.html: Pioglitazone is contraindicated in heart failure because it causes sodium and fluid retention, which can precipitate decompensation. It also causes weight gain and increases fracture risk.

C.html: Correct. An SGLT2 inhibitor with proven benefit is first choice given HFrEF and CKD. Dapagliflozin reduces HF hospitalisation and CKD progression (DAPA-HF, DAPA-CKD), is weight-neutral/losing and low-hypoglycaemia, matching his priorities.

D.html: Sitagliptin is weight-neutral and low-hypoglycaemia but confers no cardiovascular or renal outcome advantage. In a patient with HFrEF and CKD, an SGLT2 inhibitor is clearly preferred.

E.html: Insulin causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia and is reserved for when oral/injectable non-insulin options fail. It does not address his cardiorenal risk and conflicts with his stated preferences.

q: A 45-year-old woman is referred with hypertension resistant to three antihypertensives, including a thiazide. She has intermittent muscle cramps. Investigations show serum potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.0), sodium 144 mmol/L (135–145) and a mild metabolic alkalosis. Renal function is normal. Her aldosterone-to-renin ratio is markedly elevated, with suppressed plasma renin. She is not taking spironolactone. Following confirmatory saline suppression testing, adrenal CT shows a 1.2 cm left adrenal nodule with a normal right gland. What is the most appropriate next investigation to guide management?
options: Repeat aldosterone-to-renin ratio after stopping all antihypertensives
explain: This is confirmed primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome): resistant hypertension, hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, raised ARR and failure of aldosterone to suppress on saline loading. 🩺 The key decision is whether disease is unilateral (aldosterone-producing adenoma — surgically curable) or bilateral (idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia — medically managed with a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist). CT is unreliable for this distinction: a visible nodule may be a non-functioning incidentaloma while the contralateral 'normal' gland is the true source, and small adenomas may be missed. The Endocrine Society guideline therefore recommends adrenal venous sampling (AVS) to lateralise aldosterone secretion before any surgery in patients who would consider adrenalectomy — particularly those over ~35 years, in whom concurrent incidentalomas are common. Lateralisation on AVS justifies unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy; a non-lateralising result directs the patient to spironolactone or eplerenone. Proceeding straight to surgery on CT alone risks removing the wrong gland.

CT is unreliable for this distinction: a visible nodule may be a non-functioning incidentaloma while the contralateral 'normal' gland is the true source, and small adenomas may be missed. The Endocrine Society guideline therefore recommends adrenal venous sampling (AVS) to lateralise aldosterone secretion before any surgery in patients who would consider adrenalectomy — particularly those over ~35 years, in whom concurrent incidentalomas are common. Lateralisation on AVS justifies unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy; a non-lateralising result directs the patient to spironolactone or eplerenone. Proceeding straight to surgery on CT alone risks removing the wrong gland.

A.html: The diagnosis of primary hyperaldosteronism is already biochemically confirmed by the raised ARR and positive saline suppression test. Repeating the ARR adds nothing; the outstanding question is lateralisation, not confirmation.
A.text: The diagnosis of primary hyperaldosteronism is already biochemically confirmed by the raised ARR and positive saline suppression test. Repeating the ARR adds nothing; the outstanding question is lateralisation, not confirmation.

B.html: Urinary metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma. The biochemical picture (aldosterone excess, suppressed renin, hypokalaemia) is characteristic of Conn's, not catecholamine excess, so this does not guide management here.
B.text: Urinary metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma. The biochemical picture (aldosterone excess, suppressed renin, hypokalaemia) is characteristic of Conn's, not catecholamine excess, so this does not guide management here.

C.html: The dexamethasone suppression test assesses cortisol autonomy in suspected Cushing's syndrome. It is not relevant to lateralising aldosterone secretion in confirmed primary hyperaldosteronism.
C.text: The dexamethasone suppression test assesses cortisol autonomy in suspected Cushing's syndrome. It is not relevant to lateralising aldosterone secretion in confirmed primary hyperaldosteronism.

D.html: Correct. Adrenal venous sampling lateralises aldosterone hypersecretion and is recommended before adrenalectomy, since CT cannot reliably distinguish a functioning adenoma from a non-functioning nodule, especially over age 35. It determines surgery versus medical therapy.
D.text: Correct. Adrenal venous sampling lateralises aldosterone hypersecretion and is recommended before adrenalectomy, since CT cannot reliably distinguish a functioning adenoma from a non-functioning nodule, especially over age 35. It determines surgery versus medical therapy.

E.html: Operating on CT appearance alone risks removing a non-functioning incidentaloma while leaving the true aldosterone source, failing to cure the hypertension. Lateralisation with AVS should precede surgery in this age group.

q: A 52-year-old man is investigated for coarsening facial features, increasing glove and shoe size, and headaches over 3 years. He also has hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance. Examination shows prognathism, macroglossia and a bitemporal visual field defect. A random growth hormone is 8 µg/L. Which single investigation is most appropriate to confirm the biochemical diagnosis?
options: Oral glucose tolerance test with serial growth hormone measurement
explain: The clinical picture is classic acromegaly due to a growth-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma, with a bitemporal hemianopia from optic chiasm compression. 🧠 Growth hormone is secreted pulsatile, so a single random level is unreliable — it may be high in normal people (stress, exercise) or falsely reassuring between pulses. The diagnostic test is the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) with serial GH sampling. In health, a 75 g glucose load suppresses GH to <0.4 µg/L (assay-dependent). In acromegaly, GH secretion is autonomous and fails to suppress (paradoxical rise may occur). A raised, age-adjusted IGF-1 is the best single screening test and integrates GH secretion over time, but the OGTT provides dynamic confirmation. Once confirmed, MRI pituitary defines the adenoma and formal perimetry assesses the visual fields. The insulin tolerance test assesses GH/cortisol reserve in suspected deficiency; the short Synacthen and dexamethasone tests assess the adrenal axis, not GH excess.
explainHTML: The clinical picture is classic acromegaly due to a growth-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma, with a bitemporal hemianopia from optic chiasm compression. 🧠 Growth hormone is secreted pulsatile, so a single random level is unreliable — it may be high in normal people (stress, exercise) or falsely reassuring between pulses. The diagnostic test is the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) with serial GH sampling. In health, a 75 g glucose load suppresses GH to <0.4 µg/L (assay-dependent). In acromegaly, GH secretion is autonomous and fails to suppress (paradoxical rise may occur). A raised, age-adjusted IGF-1 is the best single screening test and integrates GH secretion over time, but the OGTT provides dynamic confirmation. Once confirmed, MRI pituitary defines the adenoma and formal perimetry assesses the visual fields. The insulin tolerance test assesses GH/cortisol reserve in suspected deficiency; the short Synacthen and dexamethasone tests assess the adrenal axis, not GH excess.

A.html: Correct. Because GH is secreted in pulses, autonomy is demonstrated by failure of GH to suppress below ~0.4 µg/L after a 75 g glucose load. The OGTT with serial GH is the confirmatory test for acromegaly.
A.text: Correct. Because GH is secreted in pulses, autonomy is demonstrated by failure of GH to suppress below ~0.4 µg/L after a 75 g glucose load. The OGTT with serial GH is the confirmatory test for acromegaly.

B.html: GH secretion is pulsatile, so a single random level cannot confirm or exclude acromegaly — values overlap with normal individuals under stress. Dynamic suppression testing is required instead.
B.text: GH secretion is pulsatile, so a single random level cannot confirm or exclude acromegaly — values overlap with normal individuals under stress. Dynamic suppression testing is required instead.

C.html: The insulin tolerance test provokes GH and cortisol release to assess pituitary reserve in suspected hormone deficiency. It is used to diagnose GH deficiency, not GH excess.
C.text: The insulin tolerance test provokes GH and cortisol release to assess pituitary reserve in suspected hormone deficiency. It is used to diagnose GH deficiency, not GH excess.

D.html: The short Synacthen test assesses adrenal cortisol response and diagnoses adrenal insufficiency. It has no role in confirming growth hormone excess in acromegaly.
D.text: The short Synacthen test assesses adrenal cortisol response and diagnoses adrenal insufficiency. It has no role in confirming growth hormone excess in acromegaly.

E.html: The dexamethasone suppression test evaluates cortisol autonomy in Cushing's syndrome. It does not assess the growth hormone axis and is inappropriate here.

q: A 70-year-old woman with metastatic squamous cell lung cancer is admitted confused and dehydrated. Investigations: corrected calcium 3.4 mmol/L (2.2–2.6), phosphate 0.7 mmol/L (0.8–1.5), parathyroid hormone <0.5 pmol/L (1.6–7.5), and normal renal function on admission. She is drowsy with a shortened QT interval on ECG. After 3 litres of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride over 24 hours she remains hypercalcaemic at 3.2 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
explain: This is hypercalcaemia of malignancy — the suppressed PTH excludes primary hyperparathyroidism, and squamous lung cancer typically secretes PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), driving osteoclastic bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. 🦴 First-line treatment is aggressive rehydration with IV 0.9% saline to restore volume and promote calciuresis. When calcium remains elevated after adequate fluid resuscitation, the next step is an intravenous bisphosphonate — zoledronic acid is preferred over pamidronate for its greater efficacy and faster normalisation. Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast-mediated resorption; the calcium-lowering effect takes 2–4 days and lasts weeks. Ensure the patient is rehydrated and check renal function first, adjusting dose for eGFR. Loop diuretics are no longer routinely recommended and risk worsening dehydration unless there is fluid overload. Glucocorticoids help in myeloma, lymphoma and vitamin D-mediated (granulomatous) hypercalcaemia, not PTHrP-driven disease. Cinacalcet is used in parathyroid-driven hypercalcaemia. Dialysis is reserved for severe, refractory or renal-failure cases. Denosumab is an alternative if bisphosphonate-refractory.

When calcium remains elevated after adequate fluid resuscitation, the next step is an intravenous bisphosphonate — zoledronic acid is preferred over pamidronate for its greater efficacy and faster normalisation. Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast-mediated resorption; the calcium-lowering effect takes 2–4 days and lasts weeks. Ensure the patient is rehydrated and check renal function first, adjusting dose for eGFR. Loop diuretics are no longer routinely recommended and risk worsening dehydration unless there is fluid overload. Dialysis is reserved for severe, refractory or renal-failure cases. Denosumab is an alternative if bisphosphonate-refractory.

A.html: Glucocorticoids lower calcium in vitamin D-mediated hypercalcaemia (sarcoidosis, lymphoma) and myeloma. They are ineffective in PTHrP-driven solid-tumour hypercalcaemia such as squamous lung cancer.
A.text: Glucocorticoids lower calcium in vitamin D-mediated hypercalcaemia (sarcoidosis, lymphoma) and myeloma. They are ineffective in PTHrP-driven solid-tumour hypercalcaemia such as squamous lung cancer.

B.html: Correct. After adequate rehydration, IV zoledronic acid inhibits osteoclastic bone resorption and is the standard next step when calcium remains high. Effect begins in 2–4 days; adjust dose for renal function.
B.text: Correct. After adequate rehydration, IV zoledronic acid inhibits osteoclastic bone resorption and is the standard next step when calcium remains high. Effect begins in 2–4 days; adjust dose for renal function.

C.html: Loop diuretics are no longer routinely recommended for hypercalcaemia and can worsen dehydration and electrolyte loss. They are reserved for managing fluid overload during rehydration, not as a primary calcium-lowering measure.
C.text: Loop diuretics are no longer routinely recommended for hypercalcaemia and can worsen dehydration and electrolyte loss. They are reserved for managing fluid overload during rehydration, not as a primary calcium-lowering measure.

D.html: Cinacalcet, a calcimimetic, lowers calcium in parathyroid-driven disease (primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism, parathyroid carcinoma). With suppressed PTH here, it is not indicated.
D.text: Cinacalcet, a calcimimetic, lowers calcium in parathyroid-driven disease (primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism, parathyroid carcinoma). With suppressed PTH here, it is not indicated.

E.html: Haemodialysis rapidly removes calcium but is reserved for severe, life-threatening or bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcaemia, particularly with renal failure. Her renal function is normal and a bisphosphonate should be tried first.

q: A 28-year-old man is referred with episodic headaches, palpitations, sweating and pallor, accompanied by paroxysmal severe hypertension (up to 220/120 mmHg). Plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated and CT shows a 4 cm right adrenal mass. His father died young of a 'thyroid tumour' and his mother has kidney stones. Genetic testing reveals a RET proto-oncogene mutation. Before surgical resection of the adrenal mass, which is the most important initial pharmacological step?
options: Commence phenoxybenzamine (alpha-blockade) then add a beta-blocker
Proceed urgently to adrenalectomy without medical preparation
explain: This is a phaeochromocytoma, here part of MEN 2A (RET mutation; medullary thyroid carcinoma — the father's 'thyroid tumour' — and primary hyperparathyroidism causing the mother's stones may co-segregate). 💥 The tumour secretes catecholamines causing paroxysmal hypertension and the classic triad of episodic headache, palpitations and sweating. The cardinal peri-operative principle is alpha-blockade first: phenoxybenzamine (a non-competitive alpha-antagonist) is started 10–14 days pre-operatively, with salt/fluid loading to re-expand the contracted plasma volume and prevent post-resection hypotension. Only after adequate alpha-blockade is a beta-blocker added to control reflex tachyarrhythmia. Giving a beta-blocker first is dangerous — blocking β2-mediated vasodilatation leaves α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, precipitating a hypertensive crisis. In MEN 2, the phaeochromocytoma must be resected before any thyroid or parathyroid surgery to avoid intraoperative catecholamine crisis. Calcium-channel blockers are adjuncts, not primary preparation, and steroids play no role.

The cardinal peri-operative principle is alpha-blockade first: phenoxybenzamine (a non-competitive alpha-antagonist) is started 10–14 days pre-operatively, with salt/fluid loading to re-expand the contracted plasma volume and prevent post-resection hypotension. Only after adequate alpha-blockade is a beta-blocker added to control reflex tachyarrhythmia. Giving a beta-blocker first is dangerous — blocking β2-mediated vasodilatation leaves α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, precipitating a hypertensive crisis. In MEN 2, the phaeochromocytoma must be resected before any thyroid or parathyroid surgery to avoid intraoperative catecholamine crisis. Calcium-channel blockers are adjuncts, not primary preparation, and steroids play no role.

A.html: Correct. Alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine (plus volume expansion) must precede beta-blockade. This controls catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction and prevents post-resection hypotension; the beta-blocker is added later for reflex tachycardia.
A.text: Correct. Alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine (plus volume expansion) must precede beta-blockade. This controls catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction and prevents post-resection hypotension; the beta-blocker is added later for reflex tachycardia.

B.html: Beta-blockade alone is contraindicated first: blocking β2 vasodilatation leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which can precipitate a severe hypertensive crisis. Alpha-blockade must be established beforehand.
B.text: Beta-blockade alone is contraindicated first: blocking β2 vasodilatation leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which can precipitate a severe hypertensive crisis. Alpha-blockade must be established beforehand.

C.html: Calcium-channel blockers may be used as adjuncts for residual hypertension, but they do not provide the alpha-adrenergic blockade essential for safe surgical preparation and are not the primary step.
C.text: Calcium-channel blockers may be used as adjuncts for residual hypertension, but they do not provide the alpha-adrenergic blockade essential for safe surgical preparation and are not the primary step.

D.html: Intravenous hydrocortisone treats adrenal insufficiency, not catecholamine excess. It has no role in preparing a patient with a functioning phaeochromocytoma for surgery.

E.html: Operating without adequate alpha-blockade and volume expansion risks a fatal intraoperative hypertensive crisis during tumour handling. Elective preparation over 10–14 days is mandatory unless the tumour is unstable and emergent.

q: A 74-year-old woman is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. On day 2 she is noted to have serum sodium 118 mmol/L (135–145). She is clinically euvolaemic, not on diuretics, and has normal renal, thyroid and adrenal function. Serum osmolality is 248 mosmol/kg (275–295), urine osmolality 480 mosmol/kg and urine sodium 62 mmol/L. She is alert with no seizures. Which is the most appropriate initial management of her hyponatraemia?
options: Rapid correction with 3% hypertonic saline infusion
explain: The biochemistry confirms SIADH: true hypotonic hyponatraemia (low serum osmolality) with inappropriately concentrated urine (osmolality >100 mosmol/kg) and urine sodium >30 mmol/L, in a clinically euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid, adrenal and renal function. 🌊 Pneumonia is a recognised pulmonary trigger for ADH release. Because she has chronic, asymptomatic hyponatraemia (no seizures or significant neurology), first-line treatment is fluid restriction (typically 800–1000 mL/day) alongside treating the underlying pneumonia. Correction must be gradual — no more than 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours — to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome. Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma), given as small boluses. Isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen SIADH because the retained water and natriuresis lower sodium further ('desalination'). Loop diuretics are not first-line. Tolvaptan (a vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist) is a later option if fluid restriction fails, used cautiously with close monitoring to prevent overcorrection.
explainHTML: The biochemistry confirms SIADH: true hypotonic hyponatraemia (low serum osmolality) with inappropriately concentrated urine (osmolality >100 mosmol/kg) and urine sodium >30 mmol/L, in a clinically euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid, adrenal and renal function. 🌊 Pneumonia is a recognised pulmonary trigger for ADH release. Because she has chronic, asymptomatic hyponatraemia (no seizures or significant neurology), first-line treatment is fluid restriction (typically 800–1000 mL/day) alongside treating the underlying pneumonia. Correction must be gradual — no more than 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours — to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome. Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma), given as small boluses. Isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen SIADH because the retained water and natriuresis lower sodium further ('desalination'). Loop diuretics are not first-line. Tolvaptan (a vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist) is a later option if fluid restriction fails, used cautiously with close monitoring to prevent overcorrection.

A.html: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severely symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, reduced consciousness). This alert patient does not warrant it, and rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
A.text: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severely symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, reduced consciousness). This alert patient does not warrant it, and rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.

B.html: In SIADH, isotonic saline can paradoxically lower sodium further: the kidneys excrete the sodium but retain the free water under ADH action ('desalination'). It is not appropriate first-line treatment.
B.text: In SIADH, isotonic saline can paradoxically lower sodium further: the kidneys excrete the sodium but retain the free water under ADH action ('desalination'). It is not appropriate first-line treatment.

C.html: Correct. For chronic, asymptomatic SIADH, fluid restriction to 800–1000 mL/day plus treating the cause is first-line. Aim to raise sodium gradually (<8–10 mmol/L/24h) to avoid osmotic demyelination.
C.text: Correct. For chronic, asymptomatic SIADH, fluid restriction to 800–1000 mL/day plus treating the cause is first-line. Aim to raise sodium gradually (<8–10 mmol/L/24h) to avoid osmotic demyelination.

D.html: Tolvaptan is a second-line vasopressin antagonist reserved for SIADH resistant to fluid restriction, and carries a risk of overly rapid correction. It is not the initial step here.
D.text: Tolvaptan is a second-line vasopressin antagonist reserved for SIADH resistant to fluid restriction, and carries a risk of overly rapid correction. It is not the initial step here.

E.html: Furosemide is not first-line for SIADH and risks volume depletion and further electrolyte disturbance. Fluid restriction with treatment of the underlying pneumonia is the appropriate initial approach.

q: A 41-year-old woman is investigated for episodes of confusion, sweating and tremor that occur before meals and on fasting, relieved by eating. During a supervised 72-hour fast she becomes symptomatic with a laboratory glucose of 2.0 mmol/L. Simultaneous samples show: insulin 90 pmol/L (inappropriately detectable), C-peptide 0.9 nmol/L (elevated), pro-insulin elevated, and a negative sulfonylurea screen. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is suppressed. Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
explain: This is endogenous hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, and the biochemistry during Whipple's triad points to an insulinoma. 🍬 During documented hypoglycaemia (glucose <2.2 mmol/L), insulin is inappropriately detectable, and crucially both C-peptide and pro-insulin are elevated, confirming endogenous insulin secretion. Suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate reflects the antilipolytic, anti-ketogenic action of insulin. A negative sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen excludes drug-induced secretion. Insulinomas are usually small, solitary, benign pancreatic beta-cell tumours; ~5–10% are multiple or associated with MEN 1 (with parathyroid and pituitary tumours). Localisation uses CT/MRI, endoscopic ultrasound and, if needed, selective arterial calcium stimulation; definitive treatment is surgical enucleation. The key discriminators: exogenous insulin gives high insulin but low/suppressed C-peptide (option B); sulfonylureas raise C-peptide but the drug screen is positive (option C); non-islet-cell tumour hypoglycaemia is IGF-2-mediated with suppressed insulin and C-peptide (option D); Addison's causes hypoglycaemia with low, appropriately suppressed insulin.

Suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate reflects the antilipolytic, anti-ketogenic action of insulin. A negative sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen excludes drug-induced secretion. The key discriminators: exogenous insulin gives high insulin but low/suppressed C-peptide (option B); sulfonylureas raise C-peptide but the drug screen is positive (option C); non-islet-cell tumour hypoglycaemia is IGF-2-mediated with suppressed insulin and C-peptide (option D); Addison's causes hypoglycaemia with low, appropriately suppressed insulin.

A.html: Correct. Fasting hypoglycaemia with inappropriately detectable insulin, elevated C-peptide and pro-insulin, negative sulfonylurea screen and suppressed ketones is classic for an insulinoma — an endogenous insulin-secreting pancreatic beta-cell tumour.
A.text: Correct. Fasting hypoglycaemia with inappropriately detectable insulin, elevated C-peptide and pro-insulin, negative sulfonylurea screen and suppressed ketones is classic for an insulinoma — an endogenous insulin-secreting pancreatic beta-cell tumour.

B.html: Exogenous insulin raises measured insulin but suppresses C-peptide, because injected insulin contains no C-peptide and inhibits endogenous secretion. Here C-peptide and pro-insulin are elevated, excluding this.
B.text: Exogenous insulin raises measured insulin but suppresses C-peptide, because injected insulin contains no C-peptide and inhibits endogenous secretion. Here C-peptide and pro-insulin are elevated, excluding this.

C.html: Sulfonylureas stimulate endogenous insulin, so C-peptide would also be raised, mimicking an insulinoma — but the sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen would be positive. Here the drug screen is negative.
C.text: Sulfonylureas stimulate endogenous insulin, so C-peptide would also be raised, mimicking an insulinoma — but the sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen would be positive. Here the drug screen is negative.

D.html: Non-islet-cell tumour hypoglycaemia is mediated by IGF-2 (big IGF-2), which suppresses insulin and C-peptide. The elevated insulin and C-peptide here are inconsistent with this mechanism.
D.text: Non-islet-cell tumour hypoglycaemia is mediated by IGF-2 (big IGF-2), which suppresses insulin and C-peptide. The elevated insulin and C-peptide here are inconsistent with this mechanism.

E.html: Addison's disease can cause fasting hypoglycaemia through cortisol deficiency, but insulin secretion is appropriately suppressed. Elevated insulin and C-peptide point instead to an insulin-secreting tumour.

q: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness and lethargy over several days. She has recently lost weight and craves salt. On examination she is hypotensive (88/54 mmHg), with buccal and palmar-crease hyperpigmentation. Investigations: sodium 124 mmol/L, potassium 5.9 mmol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L, urea mildly raised. She is drowsy and clinically shocked. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Await a random cortisol and short Synacthen test before treating
Oral hydrocortisone and discharge with endocrine follow-up
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg plus intravenous 0.9% saline
explain: This is an Addisonian (adrenal) crisis — the combination of hypotension/shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, weight loss, salt craving and hyperpigmentation (from ACTH/POMC-derived melanocyte stimulation) indicates primary adrenal insufficiency. ⚠️ An adrenal crisis is a medical emergency and treatment must not await confirmatory testing. The immediate management is intravenous (or IM) hydrocortisone 100 mg given at once, followed by 50–100 mg every 6 hours (or by infusion), together with rapid IV 0.9% saline to correct volume depletion and hyponatraemia, and treatment of hypoglycaemia with glucose. Take a paired sample for random cortisol and ACTH beforehand if it does not delay treatment, and arrange a short Synacthen test once stable. At high stress-dose, hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity, so fludrocortisone is not needed acutely — it is added later once the daily hydrocortisone dose falls. The hyperkalaemia corrects with steroid and fluid; targeted potassium-lowering is rarely required. Identify and treat the precipitant (often infection).

A.html: Adrenal crisis is immediately life-threatening; treatment must not be delayed for test results. Take a sample for cortisol/ACTH only if it does not hold up hydrocortisone and fluids, and confirm later with a Synacthen test.
A.text: Adrenal crisis is immediately life-threatening; treatment must not be delayed for test results. Take a sample for cortisol/ACTH only if it does not hold up hydrocortisone and fluids, and confirm later with a Synacthen test.

B.html: Fluids alone do not correct the underlying glucocorticoid deficiency driving the crisis. Hydrocortisone is essential; saline without steroid is inadequate and the patient may deteriorate.
B.text: Fluids alone do not correct the underlying glucocorticoid deficiency driving the crisis. Hydrocortisone is essential; saline without steroid is inadequate and the patient may deteriorate.

C.html: A shocked, drowsy patient in adrenal crisis needs parenteral hydrocortisone, IV fluids and inpatient monitoring, not oral therapy and discharge. Oral absorption is unreliable during vomiting and hypotension.
C.text: A shocked, drowsy patient in adrenal crisis needs parenteral hydrocortisone, IV fluids and inpatient monitoring, not oral therapy and discharge. Oral absorption is unreliable during vomiting and hypotension.

D.html: Correct. Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg plus IV 0.9% saline resuscitation (and glucose for hypoglycaemia) is the emergency treatment of adrenal crisis, given before biochemical confirmation. Repeat hydrocortisone 6-hourly and treat the precipitant.

q: A 22-year-old woman is referred with mild, persistent fasting hyperglycaemia (fasting glucose 6.8–7.4 mmol/L) noted incidentally. She is of normal weight, asymptomatic, and has never had ketosis. Her father, paternal grandmother and a sibling all have 'mild diabetes' diagnosed young and controlled by diet alone. Islet autoantibodies are negative and C-peptide is preserved. HbA1c is 47 mmol/mol. Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous glucokinase (GCK) mutation. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Commence metformin and titrate to target HbA1c
No pharmacological treatment; lifestyle advice and monitoring
explain: This is GCK-MODY (MODY 2) — a maturity-onset diabetes of the young caused by a heterozygous inactivating mutation in glucokinase, the pancreatic beta-cell 'glucose sensor'. 🧬 The defect raises the glucose set-point at which insulin is secreted, producing mild, stable, non-progressive fasting hyperglycaemia (typically 5.5–8 mmol/L) present from birth. The pattern is autosomal dominant across three generations, with negative autoantibodies and preserved C-peptide distinguishing it from type 1 diabetes. The key learning point: GCK-MODY generally requires no pharmacological treatment. Regulation is intact but 'reset' higher, so glucose-lowering drugs have little effect and do not meaningfully change the already-low risk of microvascular or macrovascular complications. HbA1c stays modestly elevated (often 42–58 mmol/mol) and lifelong. Correct genetic diagnosis avoids unnecessary insulin or oral agents and reassures the patient. The important exception is pregnancy, where management depends on whether the fetus inherits the mutation, sometimes requiring treatment to protect fetal growth. Sulfonylureas are instead the treatment of choice for HNF1A/HNF4A (MODY 3/1).

A.html: Insulin is unnecessary and inappropriate in GCK-MODY. Hyperglycaemia is mild and non-progressive with a normal set-point response, and insulin confers no benefit while risking hypoglycaemia.
A.text: Insulin is unnecessary and inappropriate in GCK-MODY. Hyperglycaemia is mild and non-progressive with a normal set-point response, and insulin confers no benefit while risking hypoglycaemia.

B.html: Metformin (and other agents) have minimal effect in GCK-MODY because the beta cell simply defends a higher glucose set-point. Treatment does not reduce the already-low complication risk.
B.text: Metformin (and other agents) have minimal effect in GCK-MODY because the beta cell simply defends a higher glucose set-point. Treatment does not reduce the already-low complication risk.

C.html: Sulfonylureas are the treatment of choice for HNF1A/HNF4A MODY, not GCK-MODY. In glucokinase MODY they add hypoglycaemia risk without meaningful benefit.
C.text: Sulfonylureas are the treatment of choice for HNF1A/HNF4A MODY, not GCK-MODY. In glucokinase MODY they add hypoglycaemia risk without meaningful benefit.

D.html: SGLT2 inhibitors have no established role in GCK-MODY, where hyperglycaemia is mild, stable and low-risk. They add cost and adverse effects without changing outcomes.

E.html: Correct. GCK-MODY causes mild, stable, non-progressive hyperglycaemia with very low complication risk. Outside pregnancy, no glucose-lowering drug is needed; lifestyle advice, reassurance and monitoring are appropriate.
